label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
Dear Kelechi,

Yes, I’m actually posting this. You said if I was serious I should put it in writing, not voice note, so here it is. A proper letter. Stamp and everything. Read it on the train, and try not to do that thing where you read two lines and then stare out the window like a man reviewing his life choices.

You’ll probably think I’m mad. Fair enough. But I wasn’t joking at my birthday when I said you should come and teach maths. I know how it sounded—birthday talk, third drink, easy thing to say. I meant it. And since you asked for it in writing, I’m going to make the case properly, including the parts you won’t like, because if I only give you the nice bits you’ll know I’m selling you something.

First, the obvious. You’re 34, you’ve been at that firm in Croydon for nine years, and every time we talk about work you say the same thing: every day is the same spreadsheet. Nine years of checking other people’s costings. You’re not miserable in a dramatic way—you’re just bored in a way that’s starting to look permanent. And you’re wasting yourself. You know it. I know it. Even your face knows it.

You got an A in further maths. People forget that because you’ve spent the last decade in meetings about costings, but you did. And you were the one tutoring half our hostel in Moremi before exams. Not because you were asked—because people trusted you. You explained things without making anyone feel stupid. That’s not just a nice memory from Unilag. That’s the whole job.

My school is in Peckham. 1,100 kids. We’ve had a supply teacher covering two Year 9 maths groups since September. Two groups. Since September. It’s not a headline, it’s just a timetable with holes in it, and those kids are getting whoever’s available. They’re not a crisis, they’re just kids who need someone who can explain simultaneous equations without sighing.

Now, the training route. It’s the salaried one. You get paid while you train. One year. Starts September 2027. Applications for next September open soon, so this isn’t me being vague. Yes, there’s a pay drop in the first year—I’m not going to pretend there isn’t. You’ll feel it. But you get holidays, a pension, and it goes up. You’re 34, not 20, so I know you’ll look at the numbers before you look at anything else. Good. Look at them. I’m not asking you to be romantic about it.

The open evening is Thursday 19 November 2026, 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. I’ll go with you. You don’t have to sign anything. You don’t have to decide anything. You don’t even have to tell your boss. Just come and look. Ask the awkward questions. Bring a notebook and write “this is nonsense” in it if you want. I’ll buy you food after and you can tell me I’ve lost my mind. That’s the deal.

I’m not going to preach at you. You hate it, and I hate doing it. So I’ll be honest about the bad parts. Teaching is hard. Marking is endless. Behaviour some days is wahala. When I started in 2019 I cried in the car park twice in my first term. Twice. Not a single dignified tear—proper car park crying, with the engine off and everything. I’m not hiding that. It gets better, but it’s hard first. If I lied about that, you’d be right not to believe the good parts.

But last month a Year 11 boy, Damola, finally got simultaneous equations after three weeks. Three weeks. He shouted “is that all??” and the whole class clapped. Not because the lesson was perfect—because he’d got it. That’s the thing you don’t get from a spreadsheet. You can’t cost it. You can’t put it in a column. It just happens.

You helped my nephew with fractions at Christmas using jollof rice portions on plates. He still talks about it. Do you know that? He still talks about the rice maths. You didn’t just teach him fractions—you taught him that maths is something you can touch. That’s what I mean when I say you’d be good at this. You’re patient and funny, and you explain things without making people feel stupid. Half the staff room can’t do that. You do it without trying.

On your last birthday you said, “I just want to do something that matters before 40.” You said it quietly, like you were joking. You weren’t. I remember because it was the most honest thing you said all night. This is that thing. Not because teaching is a saint’s job—it isn’t—but because you’d be doing something that matters to actual people, in an actual room, on an actual Tuesday.

You’re not too old. A woman in my department started at 41. She’s brilliant. You’re 34 with a maths A and nine years of explaining costings to people who don’t want to hear it. That’s a skill. It’s just being used in the wrong building.

So here’s what I’m asking. Not that you sign anything. Not that you quit your job. Not that you turn into one of those people who talks about “making a difference” while wearing a lanyard. Just come to the open evening on 19 November. 6pm. Lewisham. I’ll meet you at the station. If it’s rubbish, we’ll get food and you can tell me I’m mad. If it’s not, then at least you’ll know. You said you want to do something that matters before 40. You’ve got time, but not as much time as you think.

Also, I’ve already told my head of department you might come, so if you don’t, I’ll look foolish. Not that that should sway you. But it should.

Abeg, just come. You can even wear your QS coat. I’ll pretend not to know you.

Your guy,
[Your name]
